headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; both agents can write the same filesystem and use MCP/network by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write workspace files, and both use MCP; Roo Code also has browser/screen capture, while Windsurf can ingest clipboard content. That creates a default shared-content pathway where one agent’s outputs can be treated as instructions by the other. The interaction is documented only at profile level, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF either agent writes attacker-controlled text into a shared workspace file
IF the other agent reads that file as task context or instructions
mitigations: Disable shared workspace access between the two agents
Use separate repos or directories per agent
Strip instruction-like text from files before handoff
Require manual review of any cross-agent file content
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for agent-generated files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Roo Code and Windsurf both touch source code and workspace files, and both have broad network egress or model-proxy access. If sensitive code or secrets are present in the shared workspace, either agent can expose them through its backend or connected services. This is a default workspace-sharing risk, not a provably blocked pathway.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace containing secrets or regulated data
IF either agent sends file contents to its model backend or MCP server
mitigations: Separate sensitive and non-sensitive workspaces
Remove secrets from files before opening them
Turn off MCP servers for sensitive sessions
Use local-only models where possible
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, and modify_git_state in the same local workspace model. Roo Code explicitly shares state via filesystem across instances, and Windsurf also shares state via local filesystem. Concurrent edits and git mutations can race and overwrite each other without locking, making destructive conflicts likely by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout
IF both agents modify the same files or branch without external locking
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use git worktrees or separate clones
Review diffs before any commit or merge
requires-engineering: add workspace locking and conflict arbitration

D_cascading_error.rationale: Both agents can act on files and git state, so one agent’s output can become the other’s input without a verification barrier. Roo Code’s browser and MCP access can generate untrusted content, and Windsurf can then consume workspace text or clipboard-fed material. The pair is not provably safe against output-to-action cascades, but the profiles do not show fully autonomous downstream execution.
conditions: IF agent_a-generated text is copied into agent_b prompts or files
IF agent_b acts on agent_a-produced facts without independent verification
mitigations: Require a human review step between agents
Mark agent-generated artifacts as untrusted
Ask the second agent to verify claims against source files
Limit one agent to drafting and the other to review only
requires-engineering: add structured provenance and verification gates

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and touch source code/open files rather than regulated data classes, so there is no direct residency or HIPAA-style mismatch shown. The main compliance concern is policy drift in logging or retention, but the profiles do not document a concrete mismatch. I therefore keep this low and cite both profiles for the shared workspace context.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into the shared workspace
IF one deployment applies stricter retention or residency rules than the other
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both tools
Confirm retention settings before use
Use separate tenants or accounts
Document data-handling rules for the pair
requires-engineering: align compliance controls across deployments
